Every part carries a soft antialiased alpha (blurred mask, sigma ≈ 1.1 px at plate scale) and a pale contour halo one step lighter drawn under it (the Seuss contour, ~5 px at plate scale), with the traced vector (VTracer spline) as the alternative rendering; the rig sheet compares hard, soft+contour and vector+contour side by side before a rendering is chosen. Compared on `studies/rig-sheet-02.png` (2026-10-13): hard shows stair-stepped contours, soft and vector read as drawn lines; soft+contour is the default (keeps the stipple the vector flattens), vector reserved for parts that scale large. The puppet draws a child below its parent's z behind the parent, which is how the hair sits behind the face.

text: the production is pose-to-pose. Acting lives in key drawings the image model draws from a model sheet; the puppet draws nothing and only carries holds, breakdowns and inbetweens between consecutive keys, with the skeleton of `studies/tech-rig-01.md` as the registration tool when its toolchain is present. The expensive path is consolidated into sheets so it stays efficient: one model sheet per character, generated once and approved (turnaround front / three-quarter / side on one baseline at one scale, construction volumes, a proportion ruler in heads, the D70 expression states, a hands row), and one key sheet per shot and actor (every key the timing chart names, 4–8 keys on one plate at the model sheet's scale, numbered, each with its line of action) so a shot costs one generation per actor plus the regeneration of rejected keys. Timing charts are the motion contract (section below). A clean-up standard governs every plate before it is cut (section below). The rotation-only puppet of `studies/puppet-proof-02` and the hand rig of `rig-sheet-01/02` are the failing controls. Rubric C20–C23.
